Re: native 1.1.x — cross-quant numbers from a second pair

I’ve been running the same bake-off on our own 2x GB10 pair (EXL3 fork, your native 1.1.x line, and the technigma NVFP4 stack) — same fixed prompts, thinking off, T=0, clocks untouched, this week. Numbers you don’t have yet, since your duel was native-vs-fork:

              | your native 1.1.x | your 0.6.6+106 fork | technigma v0.6.0 NVFP4

prose decode | 40.4 | 49.1 | 43.0
code decode | 62.3 | 91.6 | 67.4
prefill 64k | 1,448 | 2,483 | 2,933
4x concurrent | 217 | 639 | 359

Three things that may save you a window:

  1. Your prefill front is worse vs the NVFP4 stack than vs the fork — technigma is ~2x you at 64k (2,933 vs 1,448). But your router-pathology diagnosis implies slope 0.662 → ~0.25 ms/tok, which would put native ahead of both. The router fix looks like the highest-leverage kernel work in the field right now.

  2. Quality note for the AZ bench: the fork fails TC-92 (tenant isolation) deterministically, and technigma is the only stack so far that is clean on both TC-51 and TC-92 (full 97, T=0, dev12). Drafted/serial equality and cache exactness don’t move those — worth checking on your line when the AZ quality battery runs.

  3. Version policy: I skipped 1.1.3 the same way you did — it carried no glm/cuda performance, and my gate is perf-gated too. The 1.1.4 watch list: #1163 + #1211 (GLM CUDA KV pages from the core pool — #1163 is mergeable-clean with all release gates ticked; #1211 stacks on it), and the #1218 slot-leak fix (merged, slated for 1.1.4 — 1 line, fixes the ring-slot leak that fails concurrent-cold serving at the 64th request). One caveat from testing the pages branch on a real pair: fp8 KV x TF_KV_PAGES are mutually exclusive today (bf16-only), so paging only becomes a serving config if paging x fp8 lands. Also watching #1168 (tensor-core fp8 decode attention, 1.5-2.3x on qwen) and #1176 (int8 prompt matmuls, -20-27% prefill) — if those generalize to GLM’s DSA rows, they attack our exact decode/prefill gaps.

One methodology trap I hit: a one-line chat-template change (a thinking reminder injected after tool results, commit 23c7b03 in the technigma repo) moved median turn time 3.4 → 4.5 s across bench builds with engine speed unchanged. Lesson learned, don’t compare medians across weeks — fixed probes only.

I appreciate the work you have posted, your TF fork is generally what I run for daily use.

Just a heads up. MiaAI Lab GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-2x-DGX-Sparks-TensorFold.

Running since Oct 9 in my own personal production :), few patches and bugfixes (mostly minor).

No loops, no issues with tools. I’m conservative, Still use 200k context and automatic compaction (2 types). But tested 900k, seems to be working, but not checked for quality.

All around great, everything from daily assistant, deep researches, auto researches to standalone multi-agent coding in multi repo complex projects and Blender 3D editing. Very reliable, including fully autonomous.

Settings (some custom from my patches):

export TENSORFOLD_LOG_SECONDS=10
export TENSORFOLD_RANDOM_SEEDS=1   # unseeded requests draw a fresh seed each (best-of-N); drop for TF's prompt-derived seeds
export TF_GLM_KEEP_EFFORT=1        # thinking-off prompts keep the effort line: same-prefix cache hits for summaries (patch 1002)

export TF_GLM_KEEP_PER_CHAT=2
export TF_GLM_CACHE_ENTRIES=48

MEMORY_RESERVE_GIB=3
PARALLEL=8
MAX_TOKENS=65536
SERVED_NAME=default

SPILL_GIB=64
SPILL_DIR=......./.cache/tensorfold-spill

To me this is still the superior model over deepseek on sparks. Don’t care what the benchmarks say.

On the high vs max thing, it’s the budget: your own wall times show max thinking ~40% longer per trial, and on the hard tasks it most likely hits the 16384/turn cap mid-think, so the answer never lands and scores as a fail, which would also explain the extra fails and safety trips. From my experience, DS will stop before GLM and declare it has a conclusion, just to be agreeable. Saying it has an answer even when it doesn’t is exactly what these synthetic benchmarks reward. GLM will just keep going until it hits your harness cap or restrictions, which scores as a fail even when it was on its way to the right answer.

As far as workflows go, “GLM’s keep churning and get steered to the conclusion” beats “Deepseek’s, I’ll decide what you meant to say, call it a conclusion, and look good on benchmarks.” I’d rather have GLM do nothing and try than have DS make helpful changes I never asked for or wanted. Sure, sometimes those changes happen to be helpful, but then it’s a gamble every turn.

posts.cooked:
Based on my current experience (processing around 400 million input tokens per day), DeepSeek requires strict constraints within the prompt; otherwise, it tends to do more than what is actually requested. Achieving the opposite - getting a model to do more - is quite difficult with GLM. Consequently, DeepSeek offers greater flexibility. As a result, its operator gains more control levers, which is a good thing.

I recently had to temporarily dismantle one of my mini-clusters (which handle GLM) to return a unit via RMA (and I’m not sure how or when that will be resolved). As a result, I set up the latest available stack of Qwen 3.8 Flash Next (GitHub - myllmbox/qwen38-flash-next-recipe: qwen38-flash-next recipe for solo GB10 · GitHub) on a third device.
In terms of both feel and speed, it is very similar to DeepSeek. It also requires prompt-based constraints and occasional instructions to “think less.”
However, it utilizes a very interesting quantization method from NVIDIA, which has significantly improved the model’s reasoning capabilities. I highly recommend giving it a try and compare with the current top open weight models.

Every patch is content-verified: its A/B’s greedy outputs are identical to the
byte across arms, the §2 content gates pass, and hardmode holds. Each has an
environment kill switch and can be dropped independently.

# Patch What it does
1 absorb-mma a prompt’s absorb_q/expand_v as tensor-core GEMMs (deep fills −6.8/−7.0/−6.9%)
2 fp8-pages fp8 KV caches on the paged-KV path
3 pagerows-fix the E4M3 tables’ page rows
4 selist-fix the prefill’s token lists stay logical (a loop bug)
5 packed-s2 two-stage packed-prompt matmuls (pp +3.4/+5.8/+6.7%)
6 exl3prompt the EXL3 prompt path in one call per pass (pp +24.5/+22.7/+23.3%)
7 attnfetch8 the latent attention’s FP8 key tiles load 8 bytes at a time, a tile ahead (pp +1.7-4.3%, tg +2.9-10.9%)
8 loaddirect each layer’s tensors read past the page cache while the previous layer packs (the load wall 103 s → 83 s)
9 moeside a decode window’s MoE shared expert on a second stream (solo +2.9%)
10 zmoe-fuse a decode window’s MoE glue fused into one block; the grouped experts without slot-row copies (c4 +4.2%)
11 zprompt the prompt experts’ main loop recompiled for 8-member column blocks, the next k-tile decoded among the current MMAs (pp +1.8-2.5%)
12 zs2 the packed prompt GEMMs’ loads fixed once a block + 8-bit codes to bf16 pairs in fewer steps (pp +1.6%)
13 zshfl the 4-bit grouped experts read every trellis word once (bit-safe; neutral on this shape — kept as the base for the next patch)

Front Ours Stock recipe Ratio

The prefill chain across four days of adoption: 1,150 → 1,434 (the one-call EXL3

Summary

tensorfold: GLM text-channel XML tool calls are returned as plain content, not parsed

Summary

When serving GLM-5.3-Flash (EXL3), tensorfold parses the model’s native (special-token) tool-call
channel correctly, but when the model emits its tool call in the text-channel XML serialization
instead, the raw XML is returned to the client as ordinary content with finish_reason=stop and
an empty tool_calls array. The client (Hermes Agent) then discards the text as an unparsable
tool-call leak, sees an “empty response”, and retries into the same deterministic output — the turn
ends with no result. To the user this looks like repeated timeouts / empty replies from a healthy model.

The two GLM formats

  • Native channel — parsed fine; response arrives with a populated tool_calls array.

  • Text channel — not parsed. The model writes the call into the visible content:

    <invoke name="session_search">
  <arg key="limit">5</arg>
  <arg key="query">firewall pc project</arg>
</invoke>

    This arrives as content verbatim, tool_calls empty.

Which format the model picks appears context-dependent (long agentic contexts with large tool
schema listings seem to bias it toward the XML form); once it picks XML for a given context it
keeps doing so across resamples, so client-side retries don’t recover.

Reproduction

Replaying a stored ~20k-token conversation (system prompt + full tool-schema list + prior
tool-call / tool-result messages) against POST /v1/chat/completions:

  • Full context, streaming and non-streaming: content contains the literal XML block above,
    finish_reason=stop, tool_calls absent. Reproduces deterministically across resamples.
  • A reduced version of the same context (~1.5k tokens, no large system prompt): the model uses the
    native channel and the call is parsed correctly.
  • Occasionally the same full context does parse — i.e. the model’s format choice flips, and the
    server only handles one of the two serializations.

Failure loop on the client side (for context)

  1. Model emits the XML tool call as content; server passes it through unparsed.
  2. Client strips known tool-call XML from the text (by design it does not execute calls that did
    not arrive on the structured channel) — content is now empty.
  3. Client classifies the turn as an empty response and retries with backoff; each retry regenerates
    the same XML, so the turn ends with no output once the retry budget is spent.

Expected behavior

Parse the text-channel XML form into structured tool_calls exactly like the native channel, so
either serialization yields a usable tool call. vLLM’s glm45 tool-call parser implements exactly
this GLM XML format and may be a useful reference.

Environment

  • Server: tensorfold (OpenAI-compatible /v1), model GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3, speculative decoding
    (draft/MTP) enabled.
  • Client: Hermes Agent, chat-completions mode (streaming and non-streaming both affected).

GLM kit (python engine): tool calls to unoffered tools are returned as plain content, not tool_calls

(Revised after checking upstream issue trackers — the root cause is narrower than “XML not parsed”.)

Summary

When serving GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3 with this kit (TensorFold engine, pinned python-0.6 build), a
tool call that names a tool not present in the request’s tools list is rejected by the
parser and its raw markup is returned to the client as ordinary content with
finish_reason=stop and an empty tool_calls array. Agent clients that strip tool-call markup
from content (as Hermes Agent does by design) then see an “empty response”, retry into the same
deterministic output, and the turn ends with no result.

This is exactly the mechanism already reported upstream:

  • ashhart/TensorFold #256 (closed Oct 2026) — “GLM tool parser leaks unoffered markup into
    assistant text content instead of stripping or handling it”. A call to an unoffered tool went
    back into the reply text. Fix landed only in the Zig engine (commit be8bccbec, from PR
    #415): a well-formed call to an unoffered tool is now returned as tool_calls under its own
    name, so the client can answer “unknown tool” and the model self-corrects. The Python engine
    is frozen (#286), so the fix will not land there.
  • MiaAI-Lab GLM kit #103 (closed) — same symptom from the agent’s perspective: “raw markup
    reaching the client looks like a normal completed answer, so the agent stops without running
    its intended tool”. Resolved as diagnostics only (patch 0115, TF_GLM_TOOL_DIAGNOSTICS=1
    logs rejections); strict offered-name validation was kept deliberately.
  • Sibling-kit evidence (MiaAI-Lab Qwen3.8-Flash-Next kit #40): “1.0.0 has the fix, TensorFold
    1.0.2 reverts it” — the behavior has flip-flopped across engine releases, so version matters.

Why it looks intermittent

Only calls to unoffered tools trigger it. Tools offered in the request parse fine in both of
GLM’s serializations (native channel and text-channel XML). Agent frameworks that load tools
on demand (a discovery tool describes a tool first, and the model then calls it without the
schema being re-offered on the wire) hit this constantly — and once the model has seen a call in
one form for a given context, it tends to repeat that form across resamples, so client-side
retries don’t recover.

Reproduction

Replaying a stored ~20k-token conversation (system prompt + full tool-schema list + prior
tool-call / tool-result messages) where the model calls a tool that was described to it
mid-conversation but is not in the request’s tools array:

  • Deterministically across resamples, streaming and non-streaming: content contains the raw
    call markup, finish_reason=stop, tool_calls absent:
    <invoke name="session_search">
  <arg key="limit">5</arg>
  <arg key="query">firewall pc project</arg>
</invoke>
  • The same call with the tool present in the request’s tools list parses correctly.

Request for this kit

  1. Port the Zig-engine fix (be8bccbec / upstream PR #415) as a patch, so unoffered but
    well-formed calls reach the client as tool_calls under their own name.
  2. Failing that, port patch 0115 (TF_GLM_TOOL_DIAGNOSTICS=1) so rejected calls are visible
    server-side instead of silently degrading to content.

Environment

  • Server kit: GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3 on 2x DGX Spark (TensorFold), python engine at the kit’s
    python-0.6 pin; speculative decoding (draft/MTP) enabled.
  • Client: Hermes Agent, chat-completions mode (streaming and non-streaming both affected).

Edit2: I think it’s looking at an older version of the repo it had downloaded so wrong version number vs what I’m serving but doesn’t look like it changes much for this bug anyway until you get to the Zig stack.

Edit3:
Can sort of be fixed via this, apparently?
In hermes’ config.yaml:

  ─ yaml           
  tools:                                                                     
    tool_search:                                                             
      enabled: off     # all tools eager — no bridge, no deferred names

Then if you just trim down your tool list to what you actually use, it still doesn’t actually increase overhead anyway.
